reporting-org.narrative: The Institute for Community Based Sociotherapy (ICBS) is a non-profit organization, established in 2019 in the Netherlands, and officially registered to work as a global expertise network, uniting professionals from different parts of the world with a passion for community-based sociotherapy. Community-based sociotherapy has been implemented in different (post-conflict) regions in Sub-Sahara Africa since 2005. Practitioners who were involved in the different countries recognized the need to team up and find ways to come up with harmonized quality standards for the CBS methodology and exchange knowledge, which led to the establishment of ICBS.

title.narrative: Connecting for Peace: A scale-up of Community Based Sociotherapy as an Integrated MHPSS and Peacebuilding Approach in the Great Lakes Region

description.narrative:
The overall objective of the CONNECT project is to contribute to peace in communities in the Great Lakes Region by implementing and mainstreaming a locally developed and locally led integrated MHPSS/PB approach’.
The consortium will do this through:
1) Implementing CBS as an effective integrated MHPSS/PB approach and lay the foundation for a regional scale-up: As part of the implementation of CBS, the focus is on increasing the number of facilitators and certified CBS trainers in the region, and setting up an accreditation system for trainers, and create recognition of harmonized quality CBS standards among stakeholders in the region.
2) Conducting research on societal issues in relation to MHPSS and PB and the effectiveness of CBS through local knowledge and experience: Localizing research is an important component of the CONNECT project, as it will turn implicit local knowledge into explicit knowledge. This way the project will increase the knowledge on relevant societal issues from the community perspective and provide evidence for stakeholders on the effectiveness of integrated MHPSS/PB approaches using indicators that are relevant in the context of the Great Lakes Region.
3) Engaging with stakeholders to mainstream the CBS approach in the Great Lakes Region: all interventions contribute to the objective of mainstreaming the CBS approach in the region. Publications of research findings, round-table meetings, conferences and linking and learning meetings will all be used to inform stakeholders at governance level on CBS.

description.narrative: A socio-group is composed by 15 members who are selected from their community, and the group is facilitated for 15 sessions, by two CBS facilitators, meeting once every week for a three hour session. These sessions contribute to the improved coping skills, increased levels of self-esteem and interpersonal communication and feelings of safety and trust among CBS participants. Most participants report immediate changes in their feelings, attitudes, behavior, and relationships with others. These changes at individual level, open the way for changes among CBS participants and people closely related to them in their psychosocial wellbeing and their interpersonal relationships in the family and community, leading to increased levels of reconciliation, and resilience.

description.narrative: CBS operates in geographically defined places, primarily neighborhoods, where people live together without necessarily forming a community in which they engage in meaningful relationships and well-functioning supportive social networks. It is practiced in sociotherapy groups (socio-groups) of on average ten to fifteen people. Groups meet on a weekly basis for approximately three hours over a period of fifteen weeks in a place located in these people’s direct living environment that group members experience as safe. Group members are identified and invited by facilitators who originate from the communities where CBS is applied. The presumption is that they have a profound understanding of the social dynamics and cultural sensitivities in the area where they facilitate groups. Sociotherapy facilitators take the group through a sociotherapy journey taking 15 weeks. Each group goes through six phases: safety, trust, care, respect, new life orientations and processing emotional memories. After concluding the cycle of 15 weeks, sociotherapy facilitators, group members, their families, neighbors and local leaders come together in a conviviality meeting. Under this output, we report all the people who joined CBS groups in each period of time.

title.narrative: Accreditation system for CBS trainers has been set up under a university and/or training center.

description.narrative:
During the implementation of CBS in different countries there have been other organizations which are also using the name ‘community-based sociotherapy’ but are implementing an approach different from the approach as developed in Rwanda since 2005 or have adapted it in a way that is not in line with the underlying philosophy of CBS. Setting up an accreditation system for CBS trainers helps to protect the quality and integrity of the approach and ensure a basis from which we can engage with different actors who are interested in implementing CBS. The system will help trainers to become certified trainers. At the same time, the accreditation system will also help identifying the training needs and capacity gaps, so that CBS professionals can work on this and improve the overall quality of their service provision.

description.narrative: In CBS groups, it is preferred to have a small number of people to allow for stronger interpersonal connections. Participants may feel safer and more willing to share openly, leading to deeper discussions and trust within the group. It also helps the facilitator to provide more personalized attention to each participant, manage group dynamics, and provide a greater sense of privacy and confidentiality. Therefore, it was decided to have between 12-15 people in one CBS group.

title.narrative: # Participants who participated in socio-groups and experience positive change in their lives in the areas of mental and psychosocial wellbeing and their engagement in peacebuilding.

description.narrative: In CBS groups, regular attendance helps maintain the continuity of the group process because each session builds on previous discussions, insights, and exercises. Missing sessions can interrupt this flow, making it harder for individuals to follow the group's progress. Additionally, consistent attendance by all members strengthens group cohesion, as participants become familiar with one another, build trust, and feel more comfortable sharing. From the past experience and evaluation done, changes may be more significant for people who attend 11 and more sessions out of the total of 15 sessions.

# Psychological supervision available for CBS professionals

description.narrative: Psychological supervision for Community-Based Sociotherapy (CBS) professionals is crucial because, in addition to working in high-stress environments, supporting individuals facing trauma, conflict, or displacement, we also take them also as the wounded healers. CBS professionals may experience vicarious trauma when working with distressed individuals if they are not helped. Psychological supervision provides them with emotional support, coping strategies, and self-care techniques to sustain their well-being.

description.narrative: Socio-group members do not get any financial incentive or sitting allowance for participating in the group sessions. The rationale for this is that it would bypass the goal of Sociotherapy, which relates to breaking the circle of victimhood and dependency, to empower people and restore their dignity, to create connectedness and group support and encourage people to remain motivated by the purpose of the group sessions and not by financial motivations. Participation through intrinsic motivation is one of the core pillars of the CBS philosophy. In addition to that, not providing sitting allowances will contribute to sustainability of the approach and ownership. However, in previous CBS projects it has been observed that after the completion of 15 sessions, many Sociotherapy groups decided to continue meeting. Not only to sustain their group cohesion, but also to initiate income generating activities together for their personal, family and community socio-economic wellbeing. Some groups started small livelihood projects and other groups saving and credit groups (e.g. Voluntary Saving and Loan Associations (VSLA). In the CONNECT project, the Sociotherapy groups developing an action plan and demonstrating a need of support in terms of capacity building regarding their socio-economic initiatives, will be supported through coaching and training, and will be linked to organizations that may be of support of their income generating activities. In addition, some support, through seed funding, might be provided to groups that have special need of support to boost their income generating initiatives. The protocol. For the socio-economic intervention will be developed, to integrate socio-economic activities without jeopardizing the CBS approach.

A mixed-methods research design, including a clustered Randomized Controlled Trial (c-RCT) to evaluate the effectiveness of CBS in the Great Lakes Region.

description.narrative:
The research team conduct a study that integrates both quantitative and qualitative research methods to collect, analyse, and interpret data. The activities implemented contributing to this outcome are related to the design and application of localized mixed-methods research. The consortium together with selected research institutions and/or universities, will work on developing the research design. The outcomes of the research will inform the consortium organizations and other stakeholders on societal issues related to MHPSS/PB and the effects of CBS as an integrated MHPSS/PB approach. At the same time, it will be a learning opportunity about the research methodology itself and how to use indicators from a local perspective.
For the quantitative part of the research, ICBS and partners will work with the national universities to develop the ‘Social Dignity Scale’, allowing organizations that implement CBS (or other trauma-informed peacebuilding approaches) to measure, in a reliable and culturally valid way, the effectiveness of the approach. This way, the consortium and academic partners will develop a scale that is relevant in the regional context and measures primary outcomes of CBS, based on the phases and principles that underpin the CBS approach and locally defined indicators of what is considered ‘peace’. Primary outcomes include improvements around experiences of safety, trust, care, respect, democracy, equality, and participation. Bottom-up community indicators will be collected in communities in Burundi, DR Congo, Uganda and Rwanda. Thereafter the tool will be developed, and psychometric analysis (exploratory factor analysis and confirmatory factor analysis) will be conducted on the datasets from each country. The confirmatory factor analysis will lead to a scale that is locally designed and validated.

title.narrative: Referral system available, which is utilized by CBS professionals to refer people with severe problems, (e.g. in relation to psychological or judicial issues) to specialized services.

description.narrative: With the belief that CBS approach cannot address all the issues, we realized that some of issues that are brought in CBS groups may need specialized or additional services. We decided to build a referral system, together with our partners, for people with severe psychological or security issues or who need judicial support. A structured process, by which, individuals in need of psychological and social support services are directed to the appropriate resources, professionals, or agencies that can provide the necessary help. This is to ensure that individuals experiencing psychological, emotional, or social difficulties and other difficulties can access the care they need in a timely and well-coordinated manner. A refferal system has been developed in the second quarter of the project implementation in rwanda, and in Uganda, where TPO Uganda has a lot of experience with referral systems, the system was reinforced and will be used as a ‘best practice’ for the CBS implementation in the other countries.
